name: Freya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 58. My husband Bernard and I rent a 140-acre farm from the county council, it's one of their starter farms, though we started thirty years ago and never moved up. We've got 220 ewes, twenty beef cattle and some spring barley. Our sons are grown, Callum's an engineer abroad and Owen works at the feed mill in town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are sheep, checking feet, moving them between the river fields. Afternoons depend on the season, it might be barley, fencing, or the council's forms, which I hate. I love the evenings in May when the lambs race along the hedge. What wears me out is the money, honestly. The rent review is next year, lamb prices were awful in September, and we've got maybe a fortnight of money in the account. I'm in the Vale Farmers' Co-op, which shares a grain dryer and sells our lambs together, and that keeps us afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the hype doesn't pan out. That's sort of what I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the co-op I'd say, right, now can we talk about the supermarkets and the rent, because that's what's squeezing us. Online I might share something from the farmers' union page. I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes, and that's the problem. We were struggling before AI was a word. The rent review could add a few thousand a year, and with a fortnight in the bank, one bad lambing could tip us over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push the co-op to bargain harder with the abattoir. We'd sell the old quad bike and make do with the one. I'd keep using the co-op's price app, which tells you roughly when to sell lambs, because that's genuinely helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat. Not scared, just worn. Like a long winter that doesn't end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the rent went up by a few thousand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to cut the cattle to ten and put the money into the sheep, which pay better on our ground. Bernard would hate it, the cattle are his. We'd probably also ask the council for a payment plan, which is humbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the squeeze, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big supermarkets set the price and we take it. And the council keeps hinting it might sell its farms to balance the books. A starter farm was meant to be a public good, not a piggy bank for a bad budget year.

say: I'd tell the co-op to focus on **supermarket prices** and the rent, not AI.
I'd share a farmers' union post online but rarely **post myself**.
think: We were **struggling before AI**, so a plateau changes nothing for us.
The **rent review** plus a fortnight of savings means one bad lambing could tip us over.
do: Push the co-op to bargain harder with the **abattoir** this autumn.
Sell the **old quad bike** and manage with one.
Keep using the co-op's **price app** to time lamb sales.
feel: **Worn out** rather than scared, like a long winter that doesn't end.
S0.quote: A starter farm was meant to be a public good, not a piggy bank for a bad budget year.
fieldNote: Her stress is **already there**: the rent review, lamb prices and a fortnight of savings.
She frames the council farm as a **public good** and blames supermarkets for the squeeze.
She already uses one **simple app** and finds it helpful, which fits her steady approach.

steps.text: Push the co-op to bargain harder with the abattoir on lamb prices
Sell the old quad bike and run the farm on one
Keep using the co-op price app to time lamb sales

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, booking, buying. That's my paperwork, isn't it? The sheep can stay hands-on for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should own any new tools together, so the benefit stays with farmers and not some tech firm. I'd say that at the AGM in March. And I'd say the council needs a rule on how it uses AI to judge tenancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a bit of it would help me. If something could do the council forms and the movement records, that's a day a month back. But the same tools will let big farms run with fewer people and undercut us on price. I'd gain a day and lose a margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try whatever the co-op tests first, probably for ordering feed and the animal movement forms. I'd wait a season to see what the neighbours find before paying for anything myself. I'd argue at the AGM for a shared licence, so we split the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit of relief about the forms, and an uneasy feeling about the prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd gain a day. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fix the bottom fence along the river, which has been on the list for three years. Or sleep. Honestly, probably sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about the council using AI on tenancies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might run our accounts through a program that says we're not viable, and that's the end of us. A person on the farms committee knows Bernard pulled half the village's cars out of the flood in 2019. A program doesn't.

say: I'd tell the co-op AGM that farmers should **own new tools together**.
I'd ask the council for a **clear rule** on using AI to judge tenancies.
think: AI doing the **council forms** would give me back about a day a month.
Bigger farms using fewer people could **undercut our prices**, so I'd lose margin.
do: Try the co-op's AI for **feed orders** and animal movement forms first.
Wait **one season** to hear neighbours' results before paying for any tool.
Argue at the AGM for a **shared licence** to split the cost.
feel: **Relief** about the forms, mixed with **unease** about prices.
S1.quote: A person on the farms committee knows Bernard pulled half the village's cars out of the flood in 2019. A program doesn't.
fieldNote: She sees **paperwork gains** first, which fits a hands-on job with some admin.
Her worry is **price pressure** from bigger, leaner farms rather than losing her own work.
Classic steady approach: **wait a season**, then adopt through the co-op.

steps.text: Try the co-op AI tool for feed orders and movement forms
Argue at the March AGM for a shared co-op AI licence
Wait one season for neighbours' results before buying any tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Robots for the sheep by 2031. I'd be 63, Bernard 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public ownership of the big things, and a proper safety net for rural people. I'd say it at the co-op, to the farmers' union, and I'd actually write to the paper this time. Loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, the AGI in 2028 runs the big estates' offices, and by 2031 robots shepherd for them day and night. Their lambs get cheaper, ours don't, and with a fortnight's savings we can't last long on losses. I think we'd be out by 2032. I'd be 64, with nowhere to go but Owen's spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd push the co-op to apply for public money to buy shared robots before the big boys corner them. I'd sell the cattle, all twenty, to clear the overdraft. I'd write to our councillor and the farmers' union about protecting council tenants. And I'd talk to Owen about whether he'd want the tenancy, or whether we hand it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared, and angry under it. It feels like we're being told to leave a party we were never really invited to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen about taking the tenancy on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, don't do it for us. Take it only if the co-op owns the robots and you get a fair price. Otherwise you'd be signing up for my life with worse odds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned wanting the co-op to buy robots. Earlier you said you'd wait for neighbours to try things. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. In a two-year world there's no time to wait, and waiting is how small farms lose. So I'd still want proof, but I'd want the co-op to get the proof, fast, for all of us together.

say: I'd call for **public ownership** of the big tools and a rural **safety net**.
I'd finally **write to the paper** and press the farmers' union.
think: Big farms get **robot shepherds by 2031** and cheaper lambs than ours.
With a fortnight's savings we'd likely be **out by 2032**, living in Owen's spare room.
do: Push the co-op to bid for **public money** for shared robots in year one.
Sell all **twenty cattle** to clear the overdraft.
Write to the councillor about protecting **council tenants**.
S2.quote: In a two-year world there's no time to wait, and waiting is how small farms lose.
fieldNote: The short warning **flips her usual caution**: she wants the co-op to move fast.
She expects to lose the **farm and home** around 2032, since robots favour big farms.
Succession for son **Owen** becomes a hard question she'd answer honestly.

steps.text: Push the co-op to apply for public money for shared robots
Sell all twenty beef cattle to clear the overdraft
Write to the councillor about protecting council farm tenants
Ask son Owen whether he wants the tenancy or not

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots three after, so 2034. That's a different feeling already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's get the co-op and the council ready instead of panicking. I'd say farmers who share machines will be fine. I'd put that in the co-op newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's tight but survivable. The AGI comes in 2031 and does our office work, robots come in 2034 when I'm 66, and Bernard and I were thinking of stepping back around then anyway. The danger is the prices dropping before we're ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to learn the AI tools properly for the records and lamb sales, once a few co-op members have tried them. I'd ask the co-op to put a little into a robot fund from every sale. We'd cut the barley, which barely pays, and rent that field out for grazing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Five years feels like enough to make a plan, if people actually make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put into a co-op robot fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two pounds a lamb. Two pounds a lamb sounds like nothing, but with a hundred and twenty farms that's real money. We'd feel it, we really would, but it beats paying a contractor who owns the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it go wrong, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the council sells the farms before 2034. Then we never get to the robot bit. That's what I'd be watching, more than the AI itself.

say: I'd tell the co-op we have **five years** to get ready, not panic.
I'd write in the newsletter that farmers who **share machines** will manage.
think: Robots in 2034 land close to when we **planned to step back**.
The real risk is **prices dropping** or the council **selling farms** first.
do: Learn the **AI record tools** once co-op members have tested them.
Put about **two pounds a lamb** into a co-op robot fund.
Stop the **barley** and rent that field out for grazing.
feel: Still **anxious**, but **steadier**, because five years allows a plan.
S3.quote: Two pounds a lamb sounds like nothing, but with a hundred and twenty farms that's real money.
fieldNote: She counts the **office AI date** and the robot date separately and maps both to retirement.
Her plan is **collective saving** through the co-op rather than personal investment she can't afford.
The council **selling its farms** worries her more than the technology.

steps.text: Learn the AI record tools after co-op members have tested them
Pay two pounds a lamb into a co-op robot fund
Stop growing barley and rent the field for grazing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots in 2039. I'd be 71. Bernard would be 73.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to do it fairly, so let's do it fairly. Shared robots, public money, training for young farmers. I'd say that to anyone at the mart who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the robots come after we've handed the farm on. The old worries remain, the rent and the council and the fortnight in the bank. But a co-op robot doing the night checks at lambing might even let us keep going a couple more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as normal. I'd back the co-op fund, smaller amounts, over longer. I'd have the serious talk with Owen and Callum about succession, because ten years is enough time to bring Owen in properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's not the AI keeping me up. It's the rent letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bringing Owen in properly look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd come weekends at first, then go half-time from the feed mill in about five years. He'd learn the robots, I'd teach him the sheep. That's a fair trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound more relaxed. Is that how you'd really feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. I've been poor for thirty years, I know how to do that. Sudden change frightens me, and ten years isn't sudden.

say: I'd say ten years is the chance to do it **fairly**, with shared robots and training.
I'd tell people at the **livestock mart** that public money should back young farmers.
think: Robots arrive after we've **handed the farm on**, so the old worries matter more.
A co-op robot doing **night checks** could help us farm a few years longer.
do: Keep **farming as normal** and keep the ewe flock at 220.
Pay **smaller amounts** into the co-op robot fund over longer.
Bring son Owen in **weekends first**, then half-time in about five years.
feel: **Uneasy**, though the **rent letter** worries her more than AI does.
S4.quote: I've been poor for thirty years, I know how to do that. Sudden change frightens me, and ten years isn't sudden.
fieldNote: Ten years turns robots from a threat into a possible **helper at lambing**.
Her calm comes from a long history of **getting by** on little money.
Succession becomes **a real plan**: Owen learns robots, she teaches sheep.

steps.text: Keep the 220-ewe flock and farm as normal
Pay smaller amounts into the co-op robot fund for longer
Bring Owen onto the farm at weekends, then half-time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time for the co-op to act, and small farms lose when there's no time. What would help is public money given to co-ops, not to individual big farms, so we can own the robots together. And a promise from the council that it won't sell the starter farms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the council. People think farmers own their land. Lots of us rent, and the landlord matters as much as any machine. If the county keeps the farms, I can face nearly anything.

headlineQuote: People think farmers own their land. Lots of us rent, and the landlord matters as much as any machine.
portrait: Freya, 58, rents a **council starter farm** with her husband Bernard: sheep, a few cattle and barley.
She has about a **fortnight of savings**, low income and a rent review coming next year.
She uses one **co-op app** now and then and waits for neighbours' results before trying more.
She wants the **co-op to own robots** and public money to fund them, and blames supermarkets and council budgets.
She moves from **alarmed** with two years' warning to **uneasy** with ten, as robots fall after succession.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time for the **co-op** to act before big farms undercut them.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** paid to co-ops so small farms can own robots together.
A promise that the council **won't sell** its starter farms.
